concepts.whyItMatters: Our sacrifice for Allah's sake results in Him strengthening our faith from within, making our commitment unshakeable through His direct intervention.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: جو لوگ سب سے اوپر اللہ کا انتخاب کرتے ہیں، وہ ان کے دلوں میں ایمان لکھ دیتا ہے - ایمان الٰہی عمل سے ان کے باطن میں مستقل طور پر درج ہو جاتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: اللہ کی خاطر ہماری قربانی کا نتیجہ یہ ہے کہ وہ ہمارے ایمان کو اندر سے مضبوط کرتا ہے، ہماری وابستگی کو اس کی براہ راست مداخلت سے ناقابل تزلزل بنا دیتا ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: للذين يختارون الله فوق كل شيء، يكتب الإيمان في قلوبهم - يصبح الإيمان منقوشاً بشكل دائم في كيانهم الداخلي بفعل إلهي.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: تضحيتنا لله تؤدي إلى تقويته لإيماننا من الداخل، جاعلاً التزامنا راسخاً من خلال تدخله المباشر.

concepts.title: Spirit from Him
concepts.coreInsight: Allah supports these believers with 'a spirit from Him' - a special divine grace, strength, and light that comes directly from Allah's own essence.
concepts.whyItMatters: When we sacrifice worldly bonds for Allah, He doesn't leave us alone but provides supernatural support to sustain us through the difficulty.
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: اللہ ان مومنین کو 'اس کی طرف سے ایک روح' کے ساتھ سہارا دیتا ہے - ایک خاص الٰہی فضل، طاقت، اور نور جو براہ راست اللہ کی ذات سے آتا ہے۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: جب ہم اللہ کے لیے دنیوی رشتے قربان کرتے ہیں، وہ ہمیں تنہا نہیں چھوڑتا بلکہ مشکل سے گزرنے کے لیے ماورائے فطرت سہارا فراہم کرتا ہے۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: يؤيد الله هؤلاء المؤمنين بـ 'روح منه' - نعمة إلهية خاصة وقوة ونور يأتي مباشرة من جوهر الله ذاته.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: عندما نضحي بالروابط الدنيوية لله، لا يتركنا وحدنا بل يوفر دعماً خارقاً للطبيعة ليدعمنا خلال الصعوبة.

concepts.title: Allah's Party
concepts.coreInsight: In contrast to Satan's party mentioned earlier, these believers form 'the party of Allah' - aligned with divine will and destined for ultimate success.
concepts.whyItMatters: Our spiritual allegiance determines our eternal group - we become part of Allah's victorious party through conscious choices that prioritize Him above all.
concepts.arabicHighlight: أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ حِزْبُ ٱللَّهِ ۚ أَلَآ إِنَّ حِزْبَ ٱللَّهِ هُمُ ٱلْمُفْلِحُونَ
concepts.coreInsight_urdu: پہلے ذکر کردہ شیطان کی جماعت کے برعکس، یہ مومنین 'اللہ کی جماعت' بناتے ہیں - الٰہی مرضی سے ہم آہنگ اور حتمی کامیابی کے لیے مقدر۔
concepts.whyItMatters_urdu: ہماری روحانی وفاداری ہمارے ابدی گروہ کا تعین کرتی ہے - ہم شعوری انتخاب کے ذریعے اللہ کی فاتح جماعت کا حصہ بنتے ہیں جو اسے سب سے اوپر ترجیح دیتے ہیں۔
concepts.coreInsight_ar: على النقيض من حزب الشيطان المذكور سابقاً، يشكل هؤلاء المؤمنون 'حزب الله' - متوافقون مع الإرادة الإلهية ومقدرون للنجاح النهائي.
concepts.whyItMatters_ar: ولاؤنا الروحي يحدد مجموعتنا الأبدية - نصبح جزءاً من حزب الله المنتصر من خلال خيارات واعية تعطيه الأولوية فوق كل شيء.

22.layer4: This verse enjoys significant scholarly consensus across Islamic schools regarding its core message, though applications differ. Sunni exegetes like Ibn Kathir explain it describes companions who fought against their own relatives at Badr and other battles, prioritizing Islam over tribal loyalties. Shia interpretation includes these examples while particularly emphasizing this principle extended to supporting Imam Ali when his right was usurped, requiring prioritizing truth over relationships with those involved. Al-Tabari discusses the Quranic context where Abu Ubaidah fought his father and Abu Bakr announced readiness to fight his son, events Shia scholars acknowledge while adding examples from later Islamic history. Both traditions agree the verse doesn't forbid kind treatment of non-Muslim relatives but prohibits loyalty that compromises faith. Al-Qurtubi and Shia jurists concur on legal rulings that Muslims may maintain family ties and financial support for non-Muslim relatives while avoiding supporting their opposition to Islam. Regarding 'spirit from Him,' Sunni scholars generally interpret it as Quranic guidance or divine help, while Shia exegesis additionally emphasizes connection to the Imams as channels of divine spirit. Both schools reference the phrase 'party of Allah' with reverence, though Shia tradition particularly emphasizes that true membership requires following the divinely appointed Imams. The consensus is that this verse establishes ultimate success comes through divine pleasure achieved by prioritizing Allah over all relationships, with both traditions agreeing this represents the highest standard of faith.

22.layer4_ar: تحظى هذه الآية بتوافقٍ علمي واسع بين المدرستين الشيعية والسنية في رسالتها الجوهرية، وإن اختلف التطبيق. فعلماء السنة كابن كثير يفسِّرون الآية بأنها تصف الصحابة الذين قاتلوا أقاربهم في بدرٍ وغيرها، مُقدِّمين الإسلام على الولاءات القبلية. ويُقرُّ علماء الشيعة بهذه الشواهد مضيفين إليها أن المبدأ نفسه امتدَّ ليشمل نصرة الإمام علي حين حيل بينه وبين حقِّه الشرعي. ويتناول الطبري الآيات السياقية حيث أعلن أبو عبيدة مبارزة أبيه، وأشار أبو بكر إلى استعداده لمقاتلة ابنه، وهي وقائع يُسلِّم بها علماء الشيعة مع إضافة نظائرها من أحداث ما بعد وفاة النبي. ويتَّفق الفريقان على أن الآية لا تُحرِّم البرَّ بالأقارب غير المسلمين لكنها تنهى عن الولاء الذي يُضرُّ بالتزام الإيمان. ويتَّفق القرطبي وفقهاء الشيعة على الأحكام المستنبطة: يجوز صون صلة الرحم والإنفاق على الأقارب غير المسلمين مع تحرُّم نصرتهم على الإسلام. وفي «الروح منه» يميل علماء السنة عموماً إلى تفسيرها بالهداية القرآنية أو المعونة الإلهية، بينما يُضيف علماء الشيعة بُعداً خاصاً يتعلَّق بالأئمة بوصفهم قنوات الروح الإلهية. ويجمع الفريقان على أن «حزب الله» عنوانٌ رفيع يستلزم الالتزام بالهداية الإلهية في كلِّ أحوال الحياة، وأن الفلاح الحقيقي لا يُقاس بمعايير الدنيا الزائلة.
22.layer1: This final verse of Surah Al-Mujadila is one of the most significant in the entire Quran regarding the nature of faith and loyalty. It declares that true believers cannot harbor affection for those who oppose Allah and His messenger, even when those opponents are their closest relatives: fathers, sons, brothers, or clan members. This was directly relevant to the early Muslim community, many of whom had family members who remained hostile to Islam. The verse then pivots from prohibition to exaltation, describing the true believers as those in whose hearts Allah has inscribed faith and whom He has strengthened with a spirit from Himself. They are pleased with Allah and He is pleased with them, they will dwell in gardens of eternal bliss, and they bear the supreme title: Hizb Allah, the Party of Allah. The term hizb, meaning party or group, here carries the highest honor. Earlier in the surah, the allies of Shaytan were called hizb al-Shaytan, and this verse provides the contrasting identity for the believers. The practical teaching of this verse is profound: genuine faith cannot coexist with active loyalty to the enemies of that faith. This does not mean cutting off kind treatment or fair dealings with non-Muslim family members, but it does mean that one's deepest allegiance, love, and support must be with those who stand with Allah and His messenger. The verse closes with the affirmation that the Party of Allah are indeed the successful ones, tieing back to verse 21 and affirming their ultimate victory.
22.layer2: Ibn Kathir provides detailed historical grounding for this verse, reporting that several companions of the Prophet were tested in exactly the manner described. Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, one of the ten promised Paradise, killed his own father Abdullah ibn al-Jarrah on the day of Badr when his father came out to fight against the Muslims. Musab ibn Umayr faced his own brother on the same battlefield. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq was prepared to fight his son Abd al-Rahman, who had not yet embraced Islam. Umar ibn al-Khattab killed his maternal uncle. These incidents, according to Ibn Kathir, are the immediate context of the words 'even though they be their fathers, or their sons, or their brothers, or their kindred.' Imam al-Tabari explains the phrase 'He has inscribed faith in their hearts' as meaning Allah has firmly established, confirmed, and sealed iman within their hearts so that no opposing force could uproot it. The word ruh, translated as 'spirit,' is interpreted by classical scholars in multiple ways: some say it refers to the Quran itself, others say it refers to divine aid and grace, and still others say it is the inner light of guidance placed in the believer's heart. Al-Qurtubi in his al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran notes that the mutual pleasure expressed between Allah and His servant, in 'Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him,' represents the highest station a servant can attain and is the ultimate success (al-fawz al-akbar). Tabari and Ibn Kathir both emphasize that 'Party of Allah' is a title of honour designating those whose allegiance is wholly to Allah.
22.layer3: Sayyid Qutb devotes extensive reflection to this verse in Fi Zilal al-Quran, describing it as drawing the absolute boundary (al-fasl al-qati) between the community of faith and all other communities. He argues that the verse is not primarily about hatred but about clarity of identity and loyalty: the believer's ultimate belonging is to Allah, and this shapes every other relationship. Qutb sees the companions' willingness to fight their own relatives as one of the most profound demonstrations of this principle in human history, and views the title Hizb Allah as the highest possible social identity a human being can carry. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in al-Tafsir al-Munir analyzes the legal and social dimensions of this verse, clarifying that it does not prohibit kind treatment, financial support, or social politeness toward non-Muslim family members, as other verses explicitly permit such conduct. Rather, it prohibits al-muwadda, which is the deep inner affection and political loyalty that would compromise a believer's commitment to the faith. Al-Zuhayli connects this to the concept of al-wala wal-bara, loyalty and disavowal, noting that classical scholars always maintained a careful distinction between social justice toward all people and spiritual-political allegiance reserved for the community of faith. In the contemporary world, scholars apply this verse to questions of identity in pluralistic societies, arguing that Muslims can be good citizens, fair neighbors, and loving family members while maintaining their ultimate religious loyalty and refusing to actively support campaigns against Islam. The verse ends by proclaiming the Party of Allah as the truly successful, identifying success not with material power but with divine pleasure and eternal reward.
